section.title: Children of God
section.sectionRationale: John lifts the readers' eyes to their identity and destiny: they are now children of God through the Father's astonishing love, and one day they will be like Christ. That hope purifies them, and John shows that those born of God practice righteousness while those of the devil practice sin, drawing a clear line between the two families.
section.thesis: Because the Father has lavished His love in making believers His children now, and because they will be like Christ when He appears, they purify themselves and practice righteousness, for the Son appeared to take away sins and destroy the devil's works, and everyone born of God, in whom God's seed abides, does not go on living in sin.
section.frameNote: Four beats: remain in Christ to be confident at His coming; the love that makes us children now and the hope of being like Him; sin as lawlessness that Christ came to take away; and the two families distinguished by righteousness and love.

verses.text: And now, little children, {{meno|remain}} in Christ, so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His {{parousia|coming}}.
If you know that He is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been {{gennao|born}} of Him.
Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called {{teknon|children}} of God. And that is what we are! The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him.
Beloved, we are now children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is.
And everyone who has this hope in Him {{hagnizo|purifies}} himself, just as Christ is pure.

units.label: Sin is lawlessness
units.note: Christ appeared to take away sins

verses.text: Everyone who practices sin practices {{anomia|lawlessness}} as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness.
But you know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin.
No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him.
Little children, let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous.
The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the very start. This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil.
Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God's {{sperma|seed}} abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God.
By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother.

meno.gloss: To remain, abide, continue, dwell. John's key word for lasting union with Christ. To remain in Him is to stay in living fellowship, and it is the ground of confidence when Christ appears, so that believers will not shrink back in shame at His coming.

parousia.gloss: Coming, arrival, presence. It became the standard term for the future coming of Christ in glory. Believers who remain in Him can await His parousia with confidence rather than shame, since they belong to Him and will be made like Him.

gennao.gloss: To beget, give birth to; in the passive, to be born. To be born of God is the new birth, a real change of family and nature. It is God's work, not ours, and it shows itself in a life of righteousness; the children reflect the character of the Father who gave them life.

teknon.gloss: Child, offspring, one born into a family. John marvels that we are called children of God, and insists it is not a mere title: that is what we are. It speaks of belonging, likeness, and inheritance, a status given purely by the Father's love.

hagnizo.gloss: To purify, make clean, consecrate. Everyone who has the hope of being like Christ purifies himself, pursuing holiness now in view of who he will be. It is an active, ongoing cleansing shaped by the pattern of Christ's own purity, not a claim to be already flawless.

anomia.gloss: Lawlessness, the state or deed of being against God's law. John says sin is lawlessness, a rebellion against God's rightful order and rule. It exposes sin as not merely weakness but defiance, which is why a settled life of sin is incompatible with being born of God.

sperma.gloss: Seed, offspring, that which is sown. God's seed abides in the one born of God, an image for the divine life or word implanted at the new birth. Because this seed remains, the child of God cannot go on living in sin; the new nature bears the family likeness.

basic.context: John points the readers to who they are: children of God, made so by the Father's amazing love. That is not just a nice title; it is what they truly are. And there is more coming: when Christ appears, they will be like Him. This hope makes them want to be pure now. John then draws a clear line: those born of God practice righteousness and love, because God's life is in them, while those who go on living in sin belong to the devil, whose works Christ came to destroy.
basic.hermeneutics: The hard verses are 3:6 and 3:9, that no one born of God keeps on sinning. Read alongside 1:8-10, which says anyone claiming to have no sin is a liar, John is not teaching sinless perfection. The Greek suggests a settled, ongoing practice of sin, a whole direction of life. A child of God does not live in unbroken, unrepentant sin, because God's seed remains in him, even though he still sins and confesses.
basic.originalLanguages: Believers are to remain, meno, in Christ so they are confident at His coming, parousia. They are born, gennao, of God and called His children, teknon. The hope of being like Him leads each to purify, hagnizo, himself. Sin is lawlessness, anomia, but God's seed, sperma, abides in the one born of God, so he does not go on sinning.
basic.typology: The image of being born of God and bearing His seed fulfils the promise of a new heart and new spirit given to God's people. Being made children who will be like the Son answers the calling of humanity to bear God's image, now restored and completed in Christ.
basic.christ: The Son of God appeared to take away sins and to destroy the works of the devil, and in Him there is no sin. Believers will be made like Him when they see Him as He is, and even now they purify themselves after the pattern of His purity. He is both the Righteous One from whom they are born and the goal into whose likeness they are being remade.
basic.god: The Father's love is lavish and transforming, making rebels into His own children. He is righteous, and His children bear His righteous likeness. He implants His own seed of life in them so that they cannot go on living in sin, showing a God who not only forgives but truly changes those He adopts.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:12-13 says those who receive Christ are born of God. Romans 8 speaks of adoption and future glory with Christ. Ezekiel 36 promises a new heart and spirit, and 1 John 3:8 names Christ's purpose to destroy the devil's works.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's story of God gathering a family reaches a height here: by love the Father makes sinners His children, implants His life in them, and promises to make them like His Son. The Son came to undo the devil's works and take away sin, so the children of God are being remade into the likeness the whole story has aimed at from the beginning.

context.literary:
The passage runs across a chapter division, and the division is unhelpful, because 2:28 to 3:10 is a single unit. It opens with a call to remain in Christ and closes with a sentence that sorts humanity into two families, 3:10. In between, John moves in a circle. He begins with the appearing of Christ, 2:28, and ends the first half with the hope of that appearing, 3:2 to 3. Then he turns to the first appearing, 3:5 and 3:8, which was 'to take away sins' and 'to destroy the works of the devil.' The verb that John uses for 'appear' is the same in 2:28, 3:2, 3:5 and 3:8, so that the whole passage is held between two appearings of the same Christ, one past and one still to come.

Alongside this runs a second pattern: pairs of statements about the 'one who practices.' Verse 4 speaks of the one who practices sin, verse 7 of the one who practices righteousness, verse 8 of the one who practices sin again, and verse 10 closes by negating the whole: anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God. Each sentence begins with a universal, 'everyone' or 'no one' or 'the one who,' in John's characteristic style of stating a principle that admits no exceptions to the kind of person he describes. The wording is sharp and symmetrical on purpose. It resembles the teaching of two ways found in Deuteronomy 30:15 and Psalm 1, with no third path between them.

The mood shifts as well. Verses 1 to 3 are tender, full of 'beloved' and 'children' and the language of astonishment. Verses 4 to 10 are blunt and diagnostic. That change in tone mirrors the double nature of the letter, which is meant both to comfort and to test, and John signals the change by calling on his readers not to let anyone deceive them, verse 7. The key to reading the whole is to see that the comfort and the testing come from the same fact: they are children of a Father whose likeness they will bear.
context.historical:
The passage stands in a setting where assurance was being undermined from two sides. On one side were the teachers who had left the fellowship and who, as the letter hints, claimed a superior knowledge of God without a corresponding life. On the other were those who might conclude from John's own earlier words, 1:8 to 10, that sin does not matter, since all sin. In a Greek-speaking world where many religious teachers promised insight and spiritual elevation, some of John's readers may have been persuaded that knowing God was a matter of enlightenment, and that conduct was a secondary concern. John answers both: the life of the Father shows in the family resemblance.

The language of fatherhood and children also had weight in that world. A child was identified with a father by name, inheritance and likeness, and people spoke of a man's character as that of his father, as when Jesus tells opponents 'You belong to your father, the devil,' John 8:44. John's talk of 'children of the devil' draws on that way of speaking. It is not racial or genetic but moral, a matter of whose character one shares.

There was also a thoroughly Jewish background. Israel knew itself as God's son, Exodus 4:22 and Hosea 11:1, and the prophets looked for a day when God would give a new heart and put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:26-27. John's readers, many of them Jewish believers and Gentiles taught from the Old Testament, would have heard in 'born of God' the fulfilment of that promise, and they would also have heard Jesus' teaching to Nicodemus about being born again, John 3:3 to 8. When he says the world does not know them because it did not know Him, he repeats Jesus' own words that the world would treat them as it treated Him because it did not know the One who sent Him, John 15:21.
context.canonical:
The passage gathers up a number of strands in the Bible's teaching on sonship and holiness. The promise of a new heart in Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 and Jeremiah 31:33 lies behind the language of birth and seed. In the Gospel of John, Jesus says that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born again, John 3:3, and the prologue says that those who received Him were given the right to become children of God, 'born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God,' John 1:12 and 13. Peter says believers have been born again of imperishable seed through the living word of God, 1 Peter 1:23, and James says God chose to give us birth through the word of truth, James 1:18.

Paul develops sonship through adoption and inheritance. God sent His Son so that we might receive adoption, Galatians 4:4 to 7, and 'all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God,' Romans 8:14 to 17. He also gives the end of the story in terms of likeness: those God foreknew He predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, Romans 8:29, and we shall bear the likeness of the heavenly man, 1 Corinthians 15:49. Philippians 3:20 and 21 says that the Lord will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.

The theme of Christ's appearing also runs through the New Testament. Colossians 3:4 says that when Christ appears we also will appear with Him in glory, and Titus 2:11 to 14 pairs the grace that has already appeared with the glorious appearance still awaited, a pairing John makes in 3:5 and 3:2. Hebrews 9:26 and 28 speaks of the same two appearances. Finally, the language about sin as lawlessness joins Paul's 'mystery of lawlessness,' 2 Thessalonians 2:7, and Jesus' warning to the 'workers of lawlessness,' Matthew 7:23, which shows how seriously the New Testament takes the idea that sin is more than a mistake.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants his readers to hold two things at once and not let go of either. The first is a staggering certainty: they are God's children now, as a present fact, and nothing the world says about them can change it. The second is a moral seriousness: the child of God is recognisable by a life that resembles the Father's, and a life of settled lawlessness is not compatible with that birth. These are not opposed. John presents the second as a consequence of the first, since a person who has been born of God has His seed within.

He also wants to take away a dangerous comfort. Some of those who had left, and perhaps some who stayed, may have reasoned that a person could have the right beliefs, or the right experiences, and still live as they pleased. John replies that the person who practises sin is of the devil, and that Christ's whole purpose was to destroy that work. The passage is therefore a corrective for false security, and it ends with the pointed statement that the one who does not love his brother is not of God.

Yet John does not write to produce fear. His words are addressed to 'beloved' and 'little children,' and the whole passage is framed by hope. The readers are meant to see that purity is not the price of belonging but the natural response of those who know where they are going. They purify themselves because they have a hope, and not in order to obtain one.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sentences that begin 'everyone who' and 'no one who' in 3:4 to 10 are descriptions of kinds of people. They are statements of what is true of those who are born of God and of those who are not, and they should not be read as commands that the reader must meet. John gives the commands elsewhere in the letter, for instance to remain in Christ, 2:28, and to love, 3:11. Here he describes what flows from the new birth.

The practical difficulty is that these descriptions are heard by believers who know that they still sin. John himself says in 1:8 that we deceive ourselves if we claim to be without sin, and in 2:1 that if anyone sins we have an advocate. So the passage cannot be taken as a standard that condemns every struggling believer. It describes the direction and character of a life. The responsible application is to ask, not whether one has ever failed, but whether one is at peace with sin, making room for it, or whether one hates it, confesses it and turns toward Christ. Believers who fall should take John's words about the advocate and the cleansing blood, 1:7 and 2:1, as the answer, and not read 3:6 and 3:9 as a sentence of exclusion.

debates.question: Does John teach that a born-again person cannot sin?

views.label: Sinless perfection
views.case: A few readers have taken 3:6 and 3:9 in their plainest sense, as meaning the born again do not sin at all in this life. The wording 'cannot go on sinning' seems absolute, and the passage says whoever sins has not seen or known Him. The main difficulty is 1:8 and 10, which says that anyone who claims to be without sin deceives himself and makes God a liar, and 2:1, which provides for the believer who sins.

views.label: Habitual or characteristic sin
views.case: Most interpreters hold that John uses the present tense for continued, characteristic action: the born-again person 'keeps on sinning,' as the BSB puts it, or 'practices sin.' In 1:9 and 2:1 the verb is in a different form that views a single act of sin, and John allows that to happen. On this view the born-again may sin but cannot make sin their way of life, because of the seed within.

views.label: An ideal drawn in absolute terms
views.case: Others suggest that John is describing what it is to be born of God in its essence, as a statement of principle, much as he says in 3:10 that there are only two families. The life that comes from God cannot produce sin, and any sin comes from what remains of the old order. This reading also fits Paul's words in Romans 7:17, where he says it is sin dwelling in him that does what he does not want.

debates.bearing: The tense argument carries the most weight, and the second and third views are compatible with it. All three agree that John is not offering a rule for measuring each believer's failures but an account of what new birth does: it changes the direction of a life and cannot coexist with a settled love of sin.

debates.question: What is the 'seed' of God that remains in the one born of God?

views.label: The Holy Spirit
views.case: Because 3:24 and 4:13 say that God lives in believers by the Spirit he has given, many take the seed as the Spirit Himself, the source of the new life. This fits John 3:5 and 6, where being born of the Spirit is the new birth.

views.label: The word of God
views.case: First Peter 1:23 speaks of being born again of imperishable seed through the living word of God, and James 1:18 says God gave birth to us by the word of truth. Since John has told his readers that what they heard from the beginning is to remain in them, 2:24, some take the seed as the gospel word that has taken root.

views.label: The new life or nature from God
views.case: A broader view holds that the seed is the divine life imparted at the new birth, the nature that Peter describes when he says we become partakers of the divine nature, 2 Peter 1:4. The image is biological: a child carries the life of its father.

debates.bearing: The three are not exclusive. In the New Testament the Spirit uses the word to give new life, and the result is a real sharing in God's own character. John's point is that what God has put in a believer is not a thing that can be sustained by effort and lost by carelessness, but a living principle that He keeps.

study.originalLanguages:
The first thing to notice is the verb in 2:28 and 3:2, phaneroo, 'to appear' or 'to be revealed,' which John uses for both comings of Christ. In 3:5 and 3:8 it describes His first appearance, and the BSB renders it 'appeared' in the first and 'was revealed' in the second. In 2:28 and 3:2 it is the second. The conjunction before it is the one that normally means 'if,' and the BSB footnote notes that the Greek can be read 'when He appears or when it appears.' The sense is not doubt that He will come but uncertainty about the time, and the grammar leaves open whether the subject is Christ or what believers will be.

The word parousia, 'coming,' in 2:28 literally means 'presence' or 'arrival,' and it was used in the Greek world for the arrival of a ruler or dignitary. Jesus uses it of His return in Matthew 24:3 and Paul in 1 Thessalonians 2:19. It appears in John's letters only here. The word 'unashamed' translates a passive verb, so that the sense is 'be put to shame away from Him,' a picture of shrinking from the Lord at His appearing, which is exactly what 'confident,' parrhesia, is set against.

In 3:1 'what manner of love' translates a word, potapos, that is a cry of astonishment. It is the word used in Matthew 8:27 for 'what kind of man is this?', and it points to a love of a kind that belongs to another world. The gift is described in the perfect tense, 'has given,' a gift whose effect continues. John also takes care to use teknon, 'child,' for believers, with its emphasis on birth and family likeness, and not huios, 'son,' which in his Gospel and letters describes Jesus. In 3:1 many manuscripts include 'and that is what we are,' and the BSB keeps it as a deliberate declaration that the status is a present fact.

The verb 'be born,' gennao, appears in the perfect tense in 2:29 and 3:9, 'has been born of Him,' which gives the sense of a birth whose result abides. The one who has been so born is distinct from Christ, as 5:18 shows, where the One who was born of God, in the BSB's reading, protects the believer. Note also that in 2:29 the word 'He' moves without warning from Christ to the Father, which is typical of John's way of treating them as sharing one life.

Finally, anomia, 'lawlessness,' in 3:4 is a strong word. It is the term used in the Greek translation of Psalm 32:1 for 'transgressions' forgiven, and Paul quotes it in Romans 4:7. The BSB footnote notes it may mean 'violation of the Law.' John uses it to say that sin is not a neutral mistake but a refusal of God's authority, and it links with the 'lawless one' of 2 Thessalonians 2:8. Thus the 'practice' of sin in 3:4, in the present tense, is the ongoing active rebellion that the Son came to undo.

typology.type: Israel as God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22 and Hosea 11:1
typology.fulfillment: God called Israel His son and brought him out of Egypt, and the prophets spoke of the nation as a child loved from its youth. John applies the same language to believers: 'we are now children of God.' The correspondence is deepened in Christ, who is the true Son and who, in Hosea's words, is called out of Egypt, as Matthew 2:15 says. Through Him others are brought into the family by adoption, Galatians 4:4 to 7 and Romans 8:14 to 17. The escalation is from a nation to a family drawn from every nation, and from a status that could be lost through disobedience to a sonship secured by new birth. The type falls short because Israel as a whole did not have the heart to be a faithful son.

typology.type: The new heart and the Spirit within, Ezekiel 36:26 and 27
typology.fulfillment: God promised to remove the heart of stone, give a heart of flesh and put His Spirit within His people so that they would walk in His statutes. John's description of God's seed remaining in the born-again person, so that the person cannot continue in sin, is the inner change that the prophet looked forward to. Jesus speaks of the same promise in His words to Nicodemus about being born of water and the Spirit, John 3:5. The promise is fulfilled as a new birth and not a reform of the old heart, and the change comes from within and not from outward law. It remains incomplete in this life, since believers still struggle, as Galatians 5:17 describes.

typology.type: Seeing God and being transformed, Exodus 33:20 and Psalm 17:15
typology.fulfillment: No one could see God's face and live, and the psalmist can only hope to behold it when he awakes. John promises that 'we will see Him as He is,' and that sight will make us like Him. It is a threshold the Old Testament saints could not cross. The escalation comes with Christ, 'the one and only Son from the Father,' John 1:14, in whom the glory is seen, and the final fulfilment is in Revelation 22:4, 'They will see His face.' Even now Paul says we are being transformed into His image as we behold the Lord's glory, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The type is not yet complete: seeing and likeness are the future of the believer, and the present life holds only the beginning.

typology.type: The scapegoat that bears sin away, Leviticus 16:21 and 22
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement the sins of Israel were confessed over a goat that carried them into the wilderness. John says Christ appeared 'to take away sins,' using the verb that John the Baptist uses of the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29. The escalation in Christ is that the sins are removed by the One who is sinless and who bore them in His own body, and the removal is real and not symbolic, Hebrews 9:26. The pattern falls short in that the goat was a repeated provision and an animal, while the Son appeared once for all and gave Himself.

study.christ:
John's way of speaking about Christ in these verses is distinctive. Three times he points to Him with a word meaning 'that One,' as in 3:3, 'just as Christ is pure,' 3:5 and 3:7, 'just as Christ is righteous.' It is the language of someone who can still see Him. He sets before his readers a person with a character, and the character is the pattern for his people: pure, righteous and sinless.

The passage shows Christ's work in a sequence. He appeared 'to take away sins,' verse 5. The word for 'take away' is the one John the Baptist uses when he says the Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29, and Hebrews says He appeared 'to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself,' Hebrews 9:26. The qualification John adds, 'in Him there is no sin,' is what makes the removal possible. Paul says God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Hebrews says He was tempted in every way yet was without sin, Hebrews 4:15. Only a sinless person could carry sin away without being crushed by it.

Next, the Son 'was revealed' to destroy the works of the devil, verse 8. That is the reversal of Genesis 3, and it happens through His own death, as Hebrews 2:14 and 15 explains, and in the triumph over the powers, Colossians 2:15. What the Son did on the cross is not only forgiveness but also victory, a breaking of the enemy's hold on those who belong to Him.

The passage then looks forward to His second appearing, when 'we will be like Him.' Paul describes this as being conformed to the image of the Son so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers, Romans 8:29, and Colossians 3:4 says that when Christ who is our life appears, we will appear with Him in glory. Jesus is therefore both the one who makes sonship possible and the pattern into which sons are being remade. He is the elder brother, to use the picture, who shares His Father with us: 'My Father and your Father,' John 20:17.

There is also the gentle note that Christ is the Righteous One. In 2:1 He is our advocate, and in 2:29 and 3:7 He is the standard of righteousness. Isaiah calls Him the righteous Servant who justifies many, Isaiah 53:11, and Peter calls Him the Righteous One, Acts 3:14 in a similar line. John does not tell us to be righteous in order to become children, but to be righteous because we are born of One who is.

The caution is that the passage does not claim that the believer's purifying makes him like Christ in the way that Christ is pure by nature. The text says we purify ourselves 'just as Christ is pure,' which sets Him as the pattern and not as an equal.
study.god:
The Father's love is the first thing the passage presents about God, and it is shown as a gift: 'what manner of love the Father has given to us.' The gift is not a feeling directed toward us from a distance but a new relationship. God does not only forgive rebels; He makes them His children. Paul puts it as adoption through Jesus Christ according to the good pleasure of His will, Ephesians 1:5, and John adds that the status is real, and that is what we are. The astonishment in the verse is the right response to a God who does that.

The passage shows God as righteous. John says that Christ is righteous, and that those who practice righteousness are born of Him. The righteousness of God is not just a standard He applies from outside but a character He gives to His children. That is why John can say that those who belong to God resemble Him and those who belong to the devil resemble him. The two families are marked by family likeness and not by rule-keeping. God's holiness therefore has a missionary shape: it is a life that He gives and not only a demand He makes.

God is also the giver of life. The seed that remains in the one who has been born of Him is His own, and verse 9 gives the reason for a changed life: 'because he has been born of God.' That is a doctrine of God as the author of new creation. The same God who spoke the world into being gives a new birth, James 1:18. The final sentence of the passage, that those who do not love their brother are not of God, ties the doctrine to the next section, since the love that marks the family is the love of the Father Himself.

The passage also shows God's purpose in the Son's coming. The Son of God was revealed to destroy the works of the devil, so that God is at war with evil and wins. The devil 'has been sinning from the very start' and God does not accept this as the permanent order of things. He is neither indifferent to evil nor the author of it. At the same time, He is patient with His children, who are not yet what they will be, and He promises that what is hidden will be revealed. 'What we will be has not yet been revealed' is a sentence about God's unfinished work.

For worship, the passage gives us a reason to say 'Father' without embarrassment, and a reason to be glad about the future. It also teaches that a love so great should not leave us unchanged. To be loved in this way and to go on loving sin is a contradiction. The right response to the God of this passage is to purify ourselves in hope, and to trust that He who began the work will finish it, Philippians 1:6.

crossReferences.note: Those who receive Christ are given the right to become children of God, born not of human will but of God. It is the Gospel statement of what John says here, and it shows that the new birth is God's act and not a human achievement.

Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born again, of water and the Spirit. It explains the source of the birth that John assumes: it is the Spirit's work, and its result is a new kind of life.

God promises a new heart and a new spirit, with His own Spirit within His people so that they walk in His ways. It is the prophetic root of the seed that remains in the born-again person and of the change John describes.

Those led by the Spirit are sons of God, who cry 'Abba, Father,' and who are heirs with Christ. It parallels John 3:1 and 2 by joining present sonship to future glory, and adds that sonship brings a share in Christ's sufferings.

God predestined those He foreknew to be conformed to the image of His Son. It states the destination John describes in 3:2, that we will be like Him, and it names Jesus as the firstborn among many brothers.

As we have borne the likeness of the earthly man we shall bear the likeness of the heavenly man. It sets out the same promise with Adam as the contrast, and it shows that the likeness John expects is a bodily and complete change.

Christ appeared once to do away with sin by His sacrifice and will appear a second time to bring salvation. It gives the two appearings that John's verb joins in this passage, one to deal with sin and one to complete salvation.

John says that anyone who claims to be without sin deceives himself, and that confession brings forgiveness. It guards the reading of 3:6 and 3:9 against a claim of sinless perfection, and shows how the two statements stand together.

The believer's life is hidden with Christ in God, and when He appears we will appear with Him in glory. It matches the hope of 3:2 and 3 and gives the reason for the present hiddenness: the world does not know us because it did not know Him.

The grace of God has appeared and we await the glorious appearance of our great God and Savior, who gave Himself to redeem us from all lawlessness and purify a people for His own. It combines the two appearings and the call to purity that John joins in verse 3.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with human beings made in the image and likeness of God, Genesis 1:26 and 27, and made to be His children in the sense that they bear His likeness and live in His presence. The fall breaks that relationship. The man and woman are driven from the garden, and Genesis 5:3 notes that Adam's son was born 'in his likeness, after his image,' so the human family carries on a likeness that is damaged. John's two families in 3:10 are the result of that long division, the children of the serpent's line and the children of the woman's, which began in Genesis 3:15.

God's answer is a family. He calls Israel His son out of Egypt, and the prophets promise a day of a new heart, a new covenant and the Spirit poured out. When the time had fully come, God sent His Son, Galatians 4:4, so that those who were slaves might receive adoption. In Jesus, the true Son and the true Adam, the image of God is restored, and those who are united to Him are born again into His family. John's 'we are now children of God' is therefore the heart of the gospel stated simply: what was lost in the garden has been given back in the Son.

The passage also holds the tension of the present age. Believers are children now, and yet what they will be has not been revealed. They are in the time between the two appearings, between the Son's coming to destroy the devil's works and His coming to complete salvation. They still struggle with sin, and the world does not recognise them, yet they have the Spirit and the seed within, and a hope that purifies.

The story ends with the vision of Revelation 21 and 22, where the dwelling of God is with man and the redeemed see His face. The inheritance of the one who overcomes is stated in the same family words: 'I will be his God, and he will be My son,' Revelation 21:7. The likeness that was lost in Eden will be restored in full, and the children of God will bear the image of the heavenly man. Everything in John's short passage, the love given, the world's non-recognition, the hope, the purification and the war against the devil's works, is a piece of that larger movement toward the day when they will see Him as He is.

sermon.title: The Children of God
sermon.why: Begg preaches this section, 1 John 2:28-3:3, on the Father's love in making us His children, the hope of being like Christ, and the purity that hope produces. A clear, orthodox handling of Christian identity and destiny.

quiz.q: What does John marvel at in 1 John 3:1?

options.text: The manner of love the Father gave, that we should be called children of God, which is what we truly are.
options.note: John stands amazed at the Father's love in making believers His actual children.

options.text: That believers deserve to be called God's children by their effort.
options.note: It is the Father's love given to us, not something earned.

options.text: That the world admires and welcomes God's children.
options.note: John says the opposite; the world does not know us because it did not know Him.

options.text: That being a child of God is only a future hope, not a present reality.
options.note: John insists it is present, we are now children of God, though fuller glory is still to come.

quiz.q: What does John say believers will be when Christ appears?

options.text: Like Him, for we will see Him as He is.
options.note: Verse 3:2 promises transformation into Christ's likeness at His appearing.

options.text: Exactly the same as they are now, with no change.
options.note: John says what we will be has not yet been revealed; we will be like Him.

options.text: Absorbed into God so as to lose all individuality.
options.note: The promise is likeness to Christ, not loss of personhood.

options.text: Rewarded according to their nationality.
options.note: The transformation is into Christ's likeness for all His children, not by nationality.

quiz.q: Why did the Son of God appear, according to verse 8?

options.text: To destroy the works of the devil.
options.note: Verse 8 names the purpose: the Son came to undo the devil's works.

options.text: To leave humanity to sort out sin themselves.
options.note: He came to act decisively against sin and the devil, not to leave us alone.

options.text: To offer good advice about self-improvement.
options.note: He came to take away sins and destroy the devil's works, far more than advice.

options.text: To reward the righteous and ignore everyone else.
options.note: He came to take away sins and defeat the devil, opening the way for sinners to become children of God.

quiz.q: How should we understand 'no one born of God keeps on sinning' alongside 'if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves'?

options.text: It means a settled, unrepentant practice of sin, not the presence of any sin at all.
options.note: The present tense points to habitual sinning; believers still sin and confess, 1:8-10.

options.text: Believers can reach total sinless perfection in this life.
options.note: This contradicts 1:8-10 and the advocate provided in 2:1.

options.text: Sin does not matter for those who are born again.
options.note: John takes sin seriously; his point is that God's children do not live in it.

options.text: It is only an ideal that no one ever actually reaches.
options.note: John states it as a present reality of the born-again, not merely an unreachable ideal.

quiz.q: How are the children of God distinguished from the children of the devil (verse 10)?

options.text: By practicing righteousness and loving their brothers.
options.note: Verse 10 names righteousness and love as the marks of God's children.

options.text: By having no visible differences at all.
options.note: John says there is a clear distinction, seen in righteousness and love.

options.text: By outward religious reputation alone.
options.note: The mark is real righteousness and love, not mere reputation.

options.text: By strict rule-keeping without any love.
options.note: Righteousness matters, but John binds it with love for the brothers; rule-keeping without love is not the mark.

questions: John says, Behold what manner of love, that we are called children of God. How does resting in this given identity change the way you see yourself on a hard day?
The hope of being like Christ leads believers to purify themselves. How does what you will be one day shape the choices you make now?
The Son appeared to destroy the works of the devil. Where do you most long to see His victory over sin and evil in your own life?
God's seed abides in those born of Him, so they cannot go on living in sin. How do you tell the difference between a believer who stumbles and confesses and a life settled in unrepentant sin?
The children of God are marked by righteousness and love. Which of these two marks is God pressing on you to grow in right now, and how?

translationNotes.note: 'When Christ appears' can also read 'when it appears', as the BSB footnote notes; the sense is the same, the future manifestation at which believers are transformed into His likeness.
'Keeps on sinning' and 'continues to sin' render present tenses indicating ongoing, habitual practice, which is why it does not contradict 1:8-10, where believers still commit and confess sins.
'God's seed abides in him' pictures the divine life or word implanted at the new birth; because it remains, the child of God cannot make sin the settled practice of his life.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 1 John 2:28-3:10. Footnotes at 3:2, 3:3, 3:4, and 3:7 noted; variant renderings do not change the sense.
